  • Glomerulonephritis is very rare in animals overall and is usually acute in nature.
  • It is a recognised cause of CRF specifically in equines, and is incidentally found in cattle, sheep and goats.
  • Primary glomerulonephritis directly affects the glomeruli, while secondary forms follow disease elsewhere in the body.

posts.post_title: Furosemide dose used as a diuretic in suppor…

posts.post_title: Species predilection of interstitial nephrit…
posts.post_content: Interstitial nephritis (inflammation of the interstitial tissue of the kidney) is described as being common in which species and rare in others?

_aimcq_options.text: Common in cattle, rare in dogs
Common in dogs, rare in other animals

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Common in dogs, rare in other animals

Interstitial nephritis is very common in dogs and rare in other animals; it may be acute or chronic.

Correct Option Explanation

Causes include bacteria (E. coli, Leptospira canicola/icterohaemorrhagiae), virus (infectious canine hepatitis/adenovirus), the kidney worm Dioctophyma renale, and toxins/drugs (lead, arsenic, mercury, sulphonamides, paracetamol).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This reverses the species predilection; cattle are not the species highlighted as commonly affected.
  • Horses are not the species identified with common occurrence of interstitial nephritis in this material.
  • A specific species predilection (dogs) is explicitly stated, so equal occurrence across species is incorrect.
Know More
  • Kidney parenchyma undergoes inflammatory change with cellular infiltration blocking the tubules.
  • Leptospira canicola and L. icterohaemorrhagiae are specific bacterial causes.
  • Toxic causes include lead, arsenic and mercury poisoning.

posts.post_title: Route of infection responsible for embolic n…
posts.post_content: Embolic nephritis arises through which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Direct trauma to the renal capsule
Emboli originating from localized septic processes such as valvular endocarditis or suppurative uterine/udder lesions
Congenital malformation of the renal pelvis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Emboli originating from localized septic processes such as valvular endocarditis or suppurative uterine/udder lesions

Embolic nephritis results from emboli originating from localized septic processes, such as valvular endocarditis (in all species) or suppurative lesions in the uterus, udder, umbilicus or peritoneal cavity in cattle.

Correct Option Explanation

It may also be associated with systemic infections such as neonatal septicaemia, foal shigellosis, colibacillosis, salmonellosis, porcine erysipelas and septicaemic strangles in horses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct capsular trauma is not the described mechanism for embolic nephritis.
  • Congenital pelvic malformation is not the cause described for this specific nephritis type.
  • Chronic dehydration alone is not identified as the mechanism producing embolic nephritis.
Know More
  • Ureteritis and urethritis show abdominal pain, scanty turbid urine and painful urination.
  • Corynebacterium renale, E. coli, Staphylococcus and Proteus are causes of ureteritis/urethritis.
  • Treatment of ureteritis/urethritis is similar to that used for cystitis.

posts.post_title: Species in which urinary calculi are most co…
posts.post_content: In which species are urinary calculi (urolithiasis) most commonly found in the urinary bladder, unlike ruminants where the sigmoid flexure is the common site?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Canine

In canines, urolithiasis is more common in the urinary bladder (UB), whereas in ruminants (especially castrated males) it is more common at the sigmoid flexure of the penis.

Correct Option Explanation

Urolithiasis in general is more common in males, and calculi may be present in the kidney tubules, pelvis, ureter, bladder or urethra.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bovine (cattle) urolithiasis, particularly in castrated males, is characteristically located at the sigmoid flexure, not the bladder.
  • Ovine (sheep) urolithiasis follows the ruminant pattern with sigmoid flexure predilection in castrated males, not primarily the bladder.
  • Caprine (goat) urolithiasis similarly follows the ruminant pattern rather than the canine bladder predilection.
Know More
  • Clinical findings of urolithiasis include severe pain, stiff gait, grunting on urination, hydronephrosis and uremia.
  • Treatment involves surgical correction via urethrotomy, cystotomy or ureterotomy.
  • Dietary management in dogs focuses on changing urinary pH; in ruminants, NaCl or ammonium chloride (10 g/sheep) is used.

posts.post_title: Basic bone lesion underlying rickets
posts.post_content: What is the basic bone lesion underlying rickets in young growing animals?

_aimcq_options.text: Failure of provisional calcification with persistent hypertrophic cartilage and epiphyseal enlargement
Premature closure of the growth plate

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Failure of provisional calcification with persistent hypertrophic cartilage and epiphyseal enlargement

The basic lesion of rickets is failure of provisional calcification, with persistent hypertrophic cartilage and enlargement of the epiphysis.

Correct Option Explanation

This leads to deformity of the skeleton and disturbance in general health in young growing animals.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rickets involves defective, not excessive, calcification of growing bone.
  • Cartilage is still formed but persists abnormally (hypertrophic) rather than being entirely absent.
  • Premature growth plate closure is not the lesion described; rather the epiphyseal plate widens abnormally.
Know More
  • Rickets is caused by disturbed calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D metabolism.
  • Radiography shows a wide epiphyseal plate/line with a woolly, moth-eaten appearance.
  • Serum alkaline phosphatase is increased in rickets.

posts.post_title: Costochondral junction change described as a…
posts.post_content: Enlargement of the costochondral junctions in rickets, appearing as a 'string of beads', is known by which term?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rachitic rosary

Enlargement of the costochondral junctions, appearing as a string of beads, is termed the rachitic rosary.

Correct Option Explanation

This is a classic clinical sign of rickets reflecting defective mineralisation at the cartilage-bone junction of the ribs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Pigeon chest' describes narrowing of the chest cavity from abnormal rib bending, a separate rachitic sign.
  • 'Bow legs' describes abnormal forward and outward curvature of the long bones at the knee, not the rib finding.
  • 'Arched back' is a separate described postural change in rickets, not the costochondral finding.
Know More
  • Rachitic animals show a 'pot-bellied' abdominal appearance.
  • Deformity of pelvic bones can later cause maternal dystocia.
  • Tooth eruption is delayed, irregular and prone to rapid, uneven wear.

posts.post_content: In the specific treatment of canine rickets, at what multiple of the daily requirement is vitamin D suggested to be given on alternate days for one week?

Correct Answer: 10-12 times the daily requirement

Vitamin D therapy is suggested at 10-12 times the daily requirement, given on alternate days for one week.

Correct Option Explanation

The daily vitamin D requirement of a dog is cited as 700 IU; adequate sunlight exposure and dietary correction are also recommended.

  • 1-2 times the daily requirement is too low a multiple for the described corrective vitamin D therapy.
  • 50-60 times overstates the recommended therapeutic multiple given in this source.
  • 100 times would be a substantial overdose relative to the stated dosing strategy.
Know More
  • A change of diet to a balanced commercial food may resolve rickets within 3 weeks.
  • Organ meals such as liver, kidney, heart and cod liver oil are rich vitamin D sources.

posts.post_title: Mechanism by which renal disease contributes…
posts.post_content: Which renal mechanism is described as contributing to calcium deficiency and rickets?

_aimcq_options.text: Excess phosphorus excretion increasing calcium absorption
Overproduction of parathyroid hormone by the kidney

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reduced synthesis of 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D (calcitriol)

Renal disease contributes to calcium deficiency via reduced synthesis of 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D (calcitriol), along with reduced phosphorus excretion and acidosis from nitrogenous waste accumulation.

Correct Option Explanation

In renal disease, reduced phosphorus excretion also leads to insoluble compound formation that inhibits calcium absorption, compounding the deficiency.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Renal disease causes reduced, not excess, phosphorus excretion in this context, worsening rather than improving calcium absorption.
  • Increased renal calcium reabsorption is not the mechanism described; rather, calcium becomes less available due to acidosis and reduced calcitriol.
  • Parathyroid hormone is not described as being overproduced directly by the kidney in this mechanism.
Know More
  • Calcium 'IN' factors to blood include intestinal absorption and bone resorption.
  • Calcium 'OUT' factors include renal excretion and incorporation into bone.
  • PTH, Vitamin D and calcitonin are the hormones regulating calcium balance.

posts.post_title: Dietary habit in dogs leading to phosphorus…
posts.post_content: Which behaviour in dogs is cited as a cause of phosphorus deficiency through the formation of insoluble complexes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ingesting grass containing phytic acid

Dogs that habitually ingest grass containing phytic acid form insoluble phosphorus complexes, contributing to phosphorus deficiency.

Correct Option Explanation

Other causes of phosphorus deficiency include dietary deficiency (as in milk and dairy products) and formation of insoluble complexes with excess calcium, iron or aluminium.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Excess meat consumption is instead linked to calcium deficiency (via excess phosphorus forming insoluble calcium phosphate), not phosphorus deficiency directly.
  • Excess water intake is not cited as a cause of phosphorus deficiency in this material.
  • Bone chewing is not the behaviour identified as causing phosphorus deficiency here.
Know More
  • Vitamin D deficiency can result from dietary lack (milk, cream, egg yolk, animal fat) or insufficient sunlight in indoor dogs.
  • Steatorrhoea from liver/pancreatic disease also reduces vitamin D and calcium absorption.
  • Endoparasitism is listed among the factors contributing to calcium deficiency.

posts.post_title: Serum enzyme change used in the clinical pat…
posts.post_content: Which serum enzyme change supports a clinical pathology diagnosis of rickets?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased alkaline phosphatase

Clinical pathology in rickets shows an increased level of alkaline phosphatase enzyme, along with decreased serum calcium and phosphorus.

Correct Option Explanation

Confirmatory diagnosis relies on radiography showing a wide epiphyseal plate/line and a woolly, moth-eaten appearance of the epiphyseal ends of long bones.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alkaline phosphatase is increased, not decreased, in rickets, reflecting increased osteoblastic activity.
  • Amylase is a pancreatic enzyme and is not the biochemical marker used for diagnosing rickets.
  • Creatine kinase reflects muscle damage and is not the enzyme highlighted in rickets diagnosis here.
Know More
  • Radiographic findings are described as pathognomonic for rickets diagnosis.
  • Serum calcium and phosphorus levels are both decreased in rickets.
  • A wide epiphyseal plate is a hallmark radiographic sign.

posts.post_title: Classification category of hip dysplasia, pa…
posts.post_content: Hip dysplasia, patellar luxation and elbow dysplasia are classified under which category of causes of degenerative joint disease (DJD)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Heredity

Hip dysplasia, patellar luxation and elbow dysplasia are classified under the heredity category of DJD causes.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with the injury category (blunt trauma, athletic injury, torn ligaments) and the acquired/developmental category (osteochondritis dissecans, angular limb deformity).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Injury as a category includes blunt trauma and torn ligaments, not these specific hereditary conditions.
  • Acquired/developmental causes specifically include osteochondritis dissecans and angular limb deformity, a separate category from the hereditary conditions listed.
  • Infectious causes are not one of the three categories described in this classification of DJD aetiology.
Know More
  • DJD in dogs/cats reflects bone, muscle, tendon, ligament and joint changes from instability.
  • The body forms extra bone around unstable joints, worsening inflammation over time in a 'snowball effect'.
  • The primary clinical sign of DJD is lameness or limping.

posts.post_title: Term for degenerative joint disease resultin…
posts.post_content: In dogs and cats, bone, muscle, tendon, ligament and/or joint changes resulting from joint instability or structural unsoundness are collectively termed what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Degenerative joint disease (DJD) / osteoarthritis

Degenerative joint disease (DJD), or osteoarthritis, describes bone, muscle, tendon, ligament and joint changes from instability or structural unsoundness.

Correct Option Explanation

The body attempts to correct instability by forming extra bone around affected joints, with accompanying inflammation that worsens over time in a 'snowball effect'.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Osteomyelitis is infection/inflammation of bone marrow, a distinct condition from degenerative joint disease.
  • Osteochondritis dissecans is listed as just one specific acquired/developmental cause of DJD, not the overall disease name.
  • Panosteitis is not the term used in this source for this joint-instability-driven disease process.
Know More
  • Hereditary causes of DJD include hip dysplasia, patellar luxation and elbow dysplasia.
  • Injury causes include blunt trauma and torn ligaments.
  • The main sign of DJD is lameness or limping.

posts.post_title: Reason NSAIDs and corticosteroids should not…
posts.post_content: Why are NSAIDs generally not combined with corticosteroids (e.g. cortisone, prednisone) in managing degenerative joint disease?

_aimcq_options.text: They have identical mechanisms so combining wastes cost
They cannot be used together, unlike NSAIDs alone which contain no cortisone
NSAIDs work only in cats, corticosteroids only in dogs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: They cannot be used together, unlike NSAIDs alone which contain no cortisone

NSAIDs cannot be used together with corticosteroids such as cortisone or prednisone; NSAIDs themselves contain no cortisone.

NSAIDs are described as very decent painkillers for general pain but can sometimes cause GI upset, and senior pets need healthy kidneys/livers and regular blood testing while on them.

  • The two drug classes are not described as having identical mechanisms; the material specifically warns against combining them, not that they duplicate each other.

  • Neither drug class is restricted by species in the way described; the concern is about kidney/liver health and drug combination, not species restriction.
